title: Nuclear fission and fusion
examTip: Fission and fusion both release energy. But they work in opposite directions. Fission: a large nucleus splits into two smaller ones. Fusion: two light nuclei join into a heavier one. Know the fission fuels: U-235 or Pu-239.
introTips: Fission is what happens inside every nuclear power station today. It is proven technology.
Fusion powers stars such as the Sun. But we cannot yet use it to make electricity on a large scale.
In a chain reaction, each fission releases neutrons that can trigger more fissions. Without control, this becomes an explosion (atomic bomb). Under control, it powers a reactor.
Fusion joins two light nuclei. Some of their mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
intro: Some large nuclei can split apart. Some light nuclei can join together. Both release a huge amount of energy. Splitting a nucleus is called fission. It is used in nuclear power stations. Joining nuclei is called fusion. It powers stars such as the Sun. Scientists have been trying to use fusion on Earth for many years. It is one of the biggest engineering challenges in history.

keyPoints.heading: Nuclear fission
keyPoints.content: In nuclear fission, a large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei. The two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size. A nucleus can split on its own, but this spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. Then it splits. As it splits, it gives out 2 or 3 neutrons and gamma rays. A large amount of energy is released. The two smaller nuclei and the neutrons are the fission products. All of the fission products have kinetic energy. The most common fuels are uranium-235 (U-235) and plutonium-239 (Pu-239). These isotopes split easily after absorbing a neutron.
writeBullets: Fission: a large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size
Usually the nucleus must absorb a neutron first. Spontaneous fission is rare
It gives out 2 or 3 neutrons and gamma rays, and releases energy
All the fission products (the two smaller nuclei and the neutrons) have kinetic energy

keyTerms.def: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, usually after it absorbs a neutron; it gives out 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy
The two smaller nuclei and the neutrons made in fission; all of them have kinetic energy
A uranium isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors; it splits after absorbing a neutron

keyPoints.memTip: Fission = split. Large nucleus + neutron → two smaller nuclei + 2–3 neutrons + enormous energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to describe the process step by step. Use this order. Neutron absorbed → nucleus splits → new nuclei + more neutrons + energy.

keyPoints.heading: Chain reactions and controlling fission
keyPoints.content: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons. These neutrons can go on to trigger more fissions, which each release more neutrons. This is a chain reaction. Uncontrolled chain reaction: each fission triggers several more. The number grows exponentially → an explosive release of energy → a nuclear weapon (atomic bomb). Controlled chain reaction: in a nuclear reactor, the chain reaction is controlled to control the energy released. Some of the neutrons are absorbed, so they cannot cause more fissions. On average, one neutron from each fission goes on to cause one more fission. So the energy is released at a steady rate.
writeBullets: Chain reaction: neutrons from each fission trigger more fissions → a process that keeps itself going
Controlled: on average, each fission triggers one more → a steady energy release in a reactor
In a reactor, some neutrons are absorbed, so the chain reaction stays under control

keyTerms.def: Each fission releases neutrons that cause more fissions; controlled, it runs at a steady rate; uncontrolled, it grows rapidly and causes an explosion

keyPoints.memTip: Reactor = controlled chain reaction, steady energy. Weapon = uncontrolled chain reaction, explosion.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to draw or describe the chain reaction diagram: one fission → 2–3 neutrons → more fissions. Show why it multiplies.

keyPoints.heading: Nuclear fusion
keyPoints.content: In nuclear fusion, two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus. In this process, some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation. So fusion releases a large amount of energy. Fusion is the energy source of stars, including the Sun. Scientists are trying to use fusion to generate electricity. It has not yet been done on a large scale.
writeBullets: Fusion: two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
Some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation
Fusion is the energy source of stars, including the Sun
Fusion is not yet used to generate electricity on a large scale

keyTerms.def: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus; some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation

keyPoints.memTip: Fusion = join. Light + light → heavier + energy.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be clear on the direction. Fission splits a large nucleus. Fusion joins two light nuclei to make a heavier one.

keyPoints.heading: Comparing fission and fusion
keyPoints.content: Fission and fusion both happen in the nucleus. Both release a large amount of energy. But they work in opposite directions. - Fission splits one large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei. It usually starts when the nucleus absorbs a neutron. - Fusion joins two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. Fission is used in nuclear power stations today. Its chain reaction is controlled, so the energy is released steadily. Fusion powers stars such as the Sun. It is not yet used to generate electricity on a large scale.
writeBullets: Fission splits a large nucleus. Fusion joins two light nuclei
Both release a large amount of energy
Fission is used in nuclear power stations. Its chain reaction is controlled
Fusion powers stars such as the Sun. It is not yet used to make electricity on a large scale
keyPoints.memTip: Fission = split a large nucleus. Fusion = join two light nuclei.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to say how fission and fusion differ, and what they have in common.

0.question: In nuclear fission, what usually makes a uranium-235 nucleus split?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! The U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron. Then it splits into two smaller nuclei. It also releases 2 or 3 more neutrons.
0.wrongFeedback: Fission usually starts when a U-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron. Then it splits. It releases more neutrons and a large amount of energy.

1.question: How is the chain reaction in a nuclear reactor different from the one in a nuclear weapon?
options: In a reactor it is controlled, so energy is released steadily. In a weapon it is uncontrolled
In a reactor it is uncontrolled. In a weapon it is controlled
Only a nuclear weapon uses fission
Only a nuclear reactor gives out neutrons
1.correctFeedback: Correct! In a reactor, the chain reaction is controlled to give a steady release of energy. In a weapon, it is uncontrolled and causes an explosion.
1.wrongFeedback: Both use fission chain reactions. In a reactor, some neutrons are absorbed, so the reaction stays controlled. In a weapon, the chain reaction is uncontrolled, so it explodes.

2.question: What happens in nuclear fusion?
options: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei
A nucleus gives out an alpha particle
A neutron turns into a proton
2.correctFeedback: Correct! In fusion, two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus. Some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
2.wrongFeedback: Fusion means joining. Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus. Splitting a large nucleus is fission.

3.question: Which statement compares fission and fusion correctly?
options: Fission splits a large nucleus and fusion joins two light nuclei. Both release energy
Fission joins two light nuclei and fusion splits a large nucleus
Both split a large nucleus into smaller ones
3.correctFeedback: Correct! They work in opposite directions. Fission splits a large nucleus. Fusion joins two light nuclei. Both release a large amount of energy.
3.wrongFeedback: Fission splits a large nucleus into two smaller ones. Fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier one. Both release energy.

commonMistakes: Mixing up fission and fusion. Fission splits a large nucleus. Fusion joins two light ones. A useful memory: Fission = Fragment (split apart); Fusion = Fuse (join together).
Forgetting that fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons (not just 1). This is what makes the chain reaction possible.
examTips: For chain reaction questions, explain the process step by step. Neutron absorbed by U-235 → splits → releases 2–3 neutrons → these trigger more fissions → chain reaction.
revisionCardBullets: Fission: large, unstable nucleus (usually after absorbing a neutron) → 2 smaller nuclei + 2–3 neutrons + gamma rays + energy
The two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size. All fission products have kinetic energy
Chain reaction: each fission triggers more. Controlled (reactor) or uncontrolled (weapon)
Fusion: two light nuclei join → a heavier nucleus. Some mass may become the energy of radiation
Fusion powers stars such as the Sun
Fission is used in power stations. Fusion is not yet used on a large scale
